q: Under ACI 211.1's recommended slumps, what is the maximum slump for mass concrete?
o: 50 mm
100 mm
150 mm
200 mm
ref: ACI 211.1 Table 6.3.1 Recommended slumps
n: Mass concrete is kept stiff, 25 to 50 mm, because extra water adds heat and shrinkage in thick pours. Footings and pavements allow up to 75 mm, and beams, walls and columns up to 100 mm.

q: In strength design, what is the nominal strength of a member?
o: Its capacity after the reduction factor φ has been applied
Its calculated capacity before the strength reduction factor φ is applied
The factored load that the member must be able to carry
The service load the member carries in normal use
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Nominal strength (Mn, Vn, Pn) is computed from the section and material properties. Multiplying by φ gives the design strength, which must be at least the factored load U.

q: What is the yield point of a material such as mild steel?
o: The stress at which the material finally breaks apart
The highest stress reached anywhere on the stress-strain curve
The stress at which strain increases markedly with little or no increase in stress
The stress at which the material first starts to behave elastically
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: At the yield point mild steel stretches along a flat plateau. The yield strength fy (275 MPa for Grade 40, 415 MPa for Grade 60) is the basis of reinforced concrete design.

q: What forms in a steel or concrete member when a section yields fully in bending and starts to rotate at nearly constant moment?
o: A pin support
A construction joint
A point of inflection
A plastic hinge
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Once the whole section has yielded, it can rotate like a hinge while holding its plastic moment Mp. In plastic analysis, the structure reaches its limit load when enough hinges form to create a mechanism.

q: What is the plastic limit load of a structure?
o: The load at which enough plastic hinges form to turn the structure into a mechanism
The load at which the first fibre of the section starts to yield
The load at which the material fractures at its weakest point
The service load, taken without any load factors
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: After the first yield, a ductile structure can take more load as moment redistributes. It reaches its plastic limit load when enough hinges have formed that it can deform freely without more load.

q: Which DPWH concrete class uses the nominal mix 1 : 2½ : 5 (cement : sand : gravel)?
o: Class A
Class B
Class C
Class AA
ref: DPWH Standard Specifications (Blue Book), Item 405 concrete classes
n: The nominal mixes are Class AA 1 : 1½ : 3, Class A 1 : 2 : 4, Class B 1 : 2½ : 5 and Class C 1 : 3 : 6. The leaner the mix, the lower the strength; Class B is used for non-critical structural work such as footings and slabs on grade.

q: What is a stirrup?
o: A longitudinal bar in a column
A splice between two bars
Transverse reinforcement in a beam that resists shear and torsion
A bar that resists temperature cracking in slabs
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Stirrups wrap around the longitudinal bars of a beam, in U, closed or L shapes. They cross diagonal shear cracks and, when closed, also resist torsion.

q: What does Hooke's law state?
o: Stress is proportional to the time the load is applied
Strain stays constant however large the load becomes
Stress equals the load multiplied by the area
Stress is proportional to strain in the linear-elastic range
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: σ = Eε holds up to the proportional limit. Beyond that the curve bends and the relation no longer applies.

q: Which term describes how strongly an earthquake is felt and how much damage it causes at a particular place?
o: Intensity
Magnitude
Epicenter
Focal depth
ref: PHIVOLCS Earthquake Intensity Scale (PEIS)
n: Intensity describes the effects at a place and varies with distance; PHIVOLCS rates it from I to X on the PEIS. Magnitude measures the energy released at the focus and is one number for the whole earthquake.

q: What is a plane frame?
o: A frame built only of timber members nailed together
A frame idealized as two-dimensional, with all members and loads in one plane
A frame with no joints between its members
A three-dimensional space truss analysed as a whole
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Most building frames are analysed one plane at a time. A plane frame has three degrees of freedom per joint (two translations and one rotation).

q: For materials without a clear yield point, such as high-strength steel, how is the yield strength usually defined?
o: By the stress at fracture
By the ultimate strength divided by 2
By the 0.2% offset method
By the proportional limit
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: A line parallel to the elastic slope is drawn from 0.2% strain (0.002). Its intersection with the curve is taken as the yield strength.

q: What is the modulus of elasticity?
o: The stress at which the material yields
The strain at fracture
The ratio of lateral to axial strain
The ratio of stress to strain below the proportional limit
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: E is the slope of the straight part of the stress-strain curve and measures stiffness. For steel Es = 200,000 MPa; for concrete Ec ≈ 4,700√f'c MPa.

q: Which effect does simple plastic analysis ignore?
o: Instability and second-order (P-Δ) effects
Equilibrium of forces
The yield moment of the section
The formation of plastic hinges
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Simple plastic theory assumes perfectly plastic hinges and satisfies equilibrium, but it ignores buckling, P-Δ effects, strain hardening and fracture, which must be checked separately.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum inside bend diameter applies to a standard hook on a 25 mm main bar?
o: 4db (100 mm)
6db (150 mm)
8db (200 mm)
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 425.3.1
n: Bars from 10 to 25 mm take a 6db bend: 6 × 25 = 150 mm. 28 to 36 mm bars take 8db, and 40 to 58 mm bars 10db.

q: What is the usual difference between a stirrup and a tie?
o: They are two names for the same bar in the same kind of member
A tie is used in beams for shear, and a stirrup in slabs
A stirrup is used in beams for shear; a tie is used in columns to hold the longitudinal bars
A stirrup is always a larger bar than a tie in the same building
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Stirrups serve flexural members (beams) against shear and torsion. Ties hold column bars in place against buckling and confine the concrete.

q: What is the elastic limit?
o: The stress at which the material finally breaks
The highest stress reached anywhere on the curve
The stress where the yield plateau of steel ends
The highest stress it can take and still fully recover
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Up to the elastic limit, unloading leaves no permanent set. It is slightly above the proportional limit, and in steel the two are so close they are often treated as one.

q: Under PNS 49, what minimum yield strength does Grade 275 (Grade 40) deformed bar have?
o: 275 MPa (about 40,000 psi)
230 MPa (about 33,000 psi)
415 MPa (about 60,000 psi)
520 MPa (about 75,000 psi)
ref: PNS 49 Steel bars for concrete reinforcement
n: PNS 49 grades are named by their minimum yield in MPa: Grade 230 (33 ksi), Grade 275 (40 ksi) and Grade 415 (60 ksi). Grade 415 is the usual choice for main bars in seismic work.

q: What does plastic analysis of a structure use to find its collapse load?
o: Only the elastic stresses produced at service load
Rigid-plastic behaviour with plastic hinges, while satisfying equilibrium
Only the deflection limits of the members
Wind tunnel tests of a scale model
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Plastic analysis finds the collapse mechanism and load directly. It makes use of a ductile structure's ability to redistribute moment after first yield, which elastic analysis ignores.

q: What is fracture?
o: The first yielding of a material under increasing load
A temporary elastic deformation that disappears on unloading
The breaking of a material once its strength or deformation capacity is used up
A hairline crack that closes again when the load is removed
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Fracture ends the stress-strain curve. Ductile materials neck and deform a lot first; brittle ones break suddenly with little warning.

q: What are shores in concrete construction?
o: Permanent columns that remain part of the finished building
The steel bars placed at the bottom of a slab
The side boards that form the edges of a slab
Temporary supports that hold up formwork and fresh concrete
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Shores hold up the forms until the concrete gains enough strength. Reshoring is placing them again after forms are stripped so young slabs are not overloaded by the floors above.

q: What is the proportional limit?
o: The stress beyond which stress is no longer proportional to strain
The stress at which the material fractures
The stress at the end of the yield plateau
The highest point of the stress-strain curve
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; NSCP 2015 Vol. 1, Ch. 4
n: Up to the proportional limit the stress-strain curve is straight and Hooke's law holds. The elastic limit is just above it.
